title: NEB Class 11 Physics — Thermal Expansion — 2024
subject: physics
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Define linear, superficial, and cubical expansivity. Derive the relationship between them.
questions.solution:
**Linear expansivity (α):** fractional change in length per kelvin, ΔL = αL₀ΔT.

**Superficial expansivity (β):** fractional change in area, ΔA = βA₀ΔT.

**Cubical expansivity (γ):** fractional change in volume, ΔV = γV₀ΔT.

Relation: each side L → L(1 + αΔT), so A → A(1 + αΔT)² ≈ A(1 + 2αΔT) and V → V(1 + αΔT)³ ≈ V(1 + 3αΔT). Hence **β = 2α and γ = 3α** for isotropic solids.
questions.knowledgeNote: For metals α ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁶ K⁻¹; steel α ≈ 11 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹.
questions.answer: **Linear expansivity (α):** fractional increase in **length** per kelvin rise — α = ΔL/(LΔT); unit K⁻¹. **Superficial expansivity (β):** fractional increase in **area** per kelvin — β = ΔA/(AΔT). **Cubical expansivity (γ):** fractional increase in **volume** per kelvin — γ = ΔV/(VΔT). **Relationship:** a square of side L grows to L(1 + αΔT) per side, so A′ = L²(1 + αΔT)² ≈ L²(1 + 2αΔT) ⟹ **β = 2α**; a cube gives V′ = L³(1 + αΔT)³ ≈ L³(1 + 3αΔT) ⟹ **γ = 3α**. Hence **α : β : γ = 1 : 2 : 3**. **Deep point:** the ratio comes from the binomial expansion of (1 + αΔT)ⁿ — dimensionality multiplies the coefficient, and the neglected α² terms are ~10⁻¹⁰, safely zero.

questions.question: A steel rod 2 m long at 20°C is heated to 120°C. By how much does it expand? (α for steel = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹)
questions.knowledgeNote: ΔT in °C equals ΔT in K — never add 273 when only a temperature *change* is needed.
questions.answer: **Formula:** ΔL = αLΔT. **Substitute:** α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹; L = 2 m; ΔT = 120 − 20 = 100 K. ΔL = 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 2 × 100 = **2.4 × 10⁻³ m = 2.4 mm**. **Deep point:** steel's α ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹ makes a 2 m rod grow 1.2 mm per 50 °C — small per rod, but bridge-scale when thousands of metres are involved, which is why expansion joints exist.

questions.question: Why are small gaps left between consecutive rails of a railway track?
questions.solution:
In summer the rails expand (ΔL = αL₀ΔT). With no gap, the constrained expansion produces huge compressive stress that buckles the track sideways.

The gaps give each rail room to lengthen freely, so no thermal stress builds up.
questions.knowledgeNote: Same physics as sagging overhead power lines in summer and the rollers under bridge ends.
questions.answer: **Why gaps between rails:** rails **expand when heated** — in summer sun a long welded rail would develop enormous compressive stress (steel α ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁵ K⁻¹; a 20 m rail grows ~2.4 cm per 10 °C rise... per 100 °C, ~2.4 cm) with nowhere to go, causing **buckling (sun kinks)** that derail trains. The small gaps allow each rail to lengthen freely into the space, relieving the stress; the characteristic 'clickety-click' of older trains is the wheels crossing these expansion gaps. (Modern continuous welded rail handles this with anchored stress management instead.) **Deep point:** the gap size is αLΔT made visible — engineering does the expansion sum and leaves exactly that much room.

questions.question: A pendulum clock keeps correct time in winter but loses time in summer. Explain why.
questions.solution:
In summer the pendulum rod expands, so its length L increases. Period T = 2π√(L/g) grows with L.

Each swing takes slightly longer, so the clock ticks fewer times per hour — it **loses time**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Gridiron (compensation) pendulums pair high-α and low-α rods so the effective length stays constant.
questions.answer: **Why the clock loses time in summer:** a pendulum clock's period is **T = 2π√(L/g)** — it depends on the pendulum's **length**. In summer the higher temperature expands the pendulum rod (ΔL = αLΔT > 0), so **L increases ⟹ T increases** — each swing takes longer, the clock completes fewer oscillations per true hour, and it runs **slow (loses time)**. In winter the rod contracts, T decreases, and the clock runs fast — hence 'correct in winter, slow in summer'. **Deep point:** the T ∝ √L dependence is the whole answer — expansion's fractional length change is halved in the period change (ΔT/T = ½αΔθ), which is why the loss is minutes per season, not hours.

questions.question: What is the anomalous expansion of water? Explain its importance for aquatic life in cold climates.
questions.solution:
Water **contracts** when heated from 0°C to 4°C and only expands above 4°C — so it is densest at **4°C**, the reverse of normal behaviour.

In a freezing lake, the 4°C water sinks to the bottom while 0°C ice floats on top. The ice sheet insulates the water below, which stays liquid at 4°C — so fish and plants survive winter under the ice.
questions.knowledgeNote: Hope's apparatus demonstrates this: water in the middle of the trough stays at 4°C while top and bottom freeze.
questions.answer: **Anomalous expansion of water:** between **0 °C and 4 °C, water contracts as it is heated** (instead of expanding) — its **density reaches a maximum at 4 °C** (1000 kg/m³); above 4 °C it expands normally. The anomaly arises because heating in this range breaks open the open ice-like hydrogen-bonded structures faster than ordinary thermal expansion adds volume. **Importance for aquatic life:** in winter, surface water cools to 4 °C, becomes **densest and sinks**, displacing warmer water upward — convection continues until the whole lake is at 4 °C. Further cooling makes surface water **lighter than 4 °C water**, so it stays on top and finally freezes there; the ice layer insulates the water below, which **remains liquid at ~4 °C on the lake bed**. Fish and other aquatic life survive the winter in that 4 °C bottom layer. **Deep point:** if water were normal (densest at 0 °C), lakes would freeze from the bottom up and solidify entirely, killing aquatic life — the anomaly at 4 °C is why life under ice is possible; ice floating is the same fact seen from above.

questions.question: What is a bimetallic strip? Explain its working with one application.
questions.solution:
A strip of two metals with different expansivities (e.g. brass and invar) bonded together. On heating, the high-α side lengthens more, so the strip **bends toward the low-α side**; it straightens on cooling.

**Application:** the thermostat in an electric iron — the bending strip breaks the heating circuit at the set temperature and remakes it as it cools.
questions.knowledgeNote: Bimetallic thermometers, fire alarms, and blinkers all use the same bend-with-temperature trick.
questions.answer: **Bimetallic strip:** two strips of **different metals with different expansivities** (e.g. brass — high α, and invar/steel — low α) riveted or welded together into one strip. **Working:** when heated, the high-α metal expands more than the low-α metal; since they are bonded, the strip **bends with the high-α metal on the outside of the curve** (the longer path must be outermost). On cooling it bends the other way. The bending is repeatable and proportional to temperature. **Application:** the **thermostat** — in an electric iron, the strip's bending at a set temperature opens its contacts and cuts the heating current; as it cools it bends back and reconnects, holding the iron near the chosen temperature (also used in fire alarms and car indicator flashers). **Deep point:** the strip converts a temperature difference into a *mechanical displacement* — differential expansion is the transducer; the metal with the larger α always takes the outside of the bend, the memory hook for the direction.
